extracted.intended_audience: computer science / mathematics students and technical writers (Stanford course audience) preparing term papers, technical articles, and expositions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing clear, well-edited technical and mathematical expositions (term papers and articles) aimed at either specialist or general audiences. Emphasizes quotation use, exposition techniques, typography/notation correctness, and working with editors/proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation is appropriate when quoted words express the meaning better than you can, are beautiful/witty, touch a chord of association in readers, or are otherwise apt—but quotation used merely to show that the author is learned is ill-advised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pretentious quotation (readers detect it and are repelled). Use quotations to open/conclude chapters or to set tone; find apt quotations via Bartlett, the OED, concordances, online texts, or even self-quotation when necessary. Prefer serendipitous discovery but use systematic searches when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience adaptation and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Write to suit the intended readership (general reader vs specialist): remove or explain jargon and aim for accessibility when the venue requires it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don's Scientific American experience: editors removed jargon to make the article accessible to a general audience; this cooperative editing can improve reach. When writing for nontechnical audiences try to convey 'how it feels' to practice the subject (use intuitions and examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve technical precision in exposition and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain precise mathematical notation and typographic conventions (e.g., bracket types, log-base notation, use of lg vs log).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow editors to change notation in a way that creates ambiguity (e.g., changing 'lg' to 'log' with unclear base). Insist on correct bracket usage where square brackets have special meaning. Choose clear notation and be prepared to defend it in editing/proof stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful punctuation and grammatical choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctuation choices (commas, that/which, sentence structure, plural/singular choices like 'data') affect meaning and tone and should be used thoughtfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: preserve commas you find necessary; 'that' vs 'which' has stylistic/grammatical implications; be pragmatic about contested usages (e.g., 'data' singular vs plural) but attend to consistency and the publication's style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage in cooperative editing and proof review
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat editorial changes as potentially helpful but verify that technical content remains correct; review and negotiate edits, and obtain page proofs when mathematics is involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don negotiated extensively with Scientific American and requested proofs because many issues (typesetting of math, symbol substitutions) only become apparent on proofs; telephone or written negotiations can fix important issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread typeset proofs carefully for mathematical/typographic errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Many errors appear only at the page-proof stage (symbol metamorphoses, incorrect brackets, reversed formulae), so authors should inspect and correct proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include '1' and '0' mis-rendered, bracket/parenthesis substitutions, and last-line layout problems; authors should request proofs if heavy technical notation is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and puzzles to build intuition before presenting formal material
rubrics_metrics.description: Motivate complex results or algorithms with a worked example or puzzle so the reader develops appropriate mental structures before the formal algorithm or proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don used a puzzle to motivate an algorithm and noted this builds exactly the right mental structures; use examples to show nontriviality and to prepare readers for complicated proofs or algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose effective exposition formats (dialogue/Q&A when appropriate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonstandard formats (dialogue, Q&A) can be effective for exposition and make difficult material more readable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leslie Lamport's and Don's dialog-format works are cited as examples; use format choices intentionally to aid comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance formal and informal discussion with well-chosen examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Good technical exposition blends rigorous formalism with informal explanation and illustrative examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nilsson & Genesereth chapter praised for mixing formal and informal discussion and using typographic conventions (e.g., typewriter font for logic); aim for this balance when introducing new research-level topics to students or general readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consistent typographic conventions to aid clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt and maintain typographic conventions (fonts for code/logic, spacing in numbers, notation styles) that improve readability and disambiguation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: present logic in a 'typewriter' font; follow appropriate conventions for number grouping (commas, spaces) depending on whether the figure is in text or a formula (and follow IEEE or venue standards when required).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of micro-typographic details
rubrics_metrics.description: Small layout/typographic issues (paragraph indentation, last-line lengths, caption fitting) affect presentation and sometimes require small textual adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don noted he sometimes had to add/subtract words to make the last line length match the next paragraph's indentation; magazine copy editors may edit captions by removing 'the's from the end to make lines fit—anticipate such issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select names and terminology thoughtfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminology and chosen names for concepts matter; appropriate names aid understanding and may persist in the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don regretted some past naming choices and praised community decisions (e.g., 'NP-complete' replacing 'Polynomially-complete'); think ahead about naming clarity and community adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metaphors and biological/visual analogies when they aid understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended metaphors (e.g., 'jellyfish' for tree structures) and biological terminology can make complex structures memorable and comprehensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don used metaphors and detailed biological terms (stems, polyps, tentacles, nematocysts) to serve the reduction proof; use metaphors that fit and help convey unity in complex systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to compromise while defending essential technical choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should be willing to accept some editorial changes that improve exposition while pushing back on changes that introduce errors or ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don ultimately conceded some editorial changes were appropriate but successfully argued for corrections on technical matters; aim for cooperative resolution with editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locate apt quotations and supporting references systematically when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: When serendipity fails, use quotation dictionaries (Bartlett), the OED, concordances, and electronic searches to find contextually apt quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don used Bartlett and the OED; computer search tools (online texts) now make locating quotations and contextual occurrences much easier (search for words like 'comma' to find relevant passages).
